To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a limited set of mutations to the major coat protein (MCP) of filamentous phage can enhance high copy protein display; (ii) the mutations enhance protein display by increasing the efficiency of fusion protein packing into the phage particle; and (iii) the high tolerance of phage coat proteins for mutations suggests that they could readily evolve new properties.

we have identified the residues in the phage coat protein that enable efficient display of a protein of interest on the surface of the filamentous phage, and we have identified the mechanism by which this occurs.
we have identified a set of mutations in the phage coat that allow high copy display of fusion proteins and that these mutations can be optimized to further enhance the display.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a phage display system that allows the rapid selection of high affinity binding proteins from combinatorial libraries.
the design, construction and characterization of filamentous bacteriophages displaying large proteins on the surface of the phage particle.
the design of phage coat proteins with new functions, and the use of phage display for protein discovery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the high copy protein displaying phage variants are the product of mutations in the phage coat protein that allow for better packing into the coat protein.
the high copy display phenotype of opti‐P‐8 is the result of a series of mutations that allow for more efficient packing of the fusion proteins into the phage capsid.

the mutations that promote high‐copy protein display on phage coat proteins are additive and that these mutations are localized to a hydrophobic face of the phage coat protein that is thought to be in direct contact with the phages coat.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can use phage to display any protein, and that we can optimize the display for any protein.
we are able to use phage coat proteins to create a variety of different types of display particles, and we are able to do so in a way that is very efficient and very high copy.
the phage coat protein has a very flexible structure, which is consistent with a previous study by the Caspar lab.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to evolve the phage coat proteins to allow for high‐level display of proteins fused to the N‐terminus of the coat proteins.
the M13 coat protein is a highly versatile protein scaffold, and the high copy protein‐display variants we developed are a valuable resource for the protein engineering community.
it is possible to engineer the phage coat proteins to display proteins with high copy number.
